records.source: Καὶ εἰσελθὼν διήρχετο τὴν Ἰεριχώ.
records.gloss: And having entered he was passing through the Jericho.
pieces: Jesus entered Jericho and was making {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} way through the town.

L.1: And having entered, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was passing through Jericho.

R.1: Jesus came to the town of Jericho and was walking through it.

decisions.choice: Jericho: a town in the Jordan valley, on the road up to Jerusalem
alternatives: the ancient ruined city of Joshua's time
decisions.reason: Jericho lay about fifteen miles northeast of Jerusalem and some three thousand feet lower. Pilgrims from Galilee who came down the Jordan valley went up to Jerusalem from there (10:30; 18:35). It was a rich town, with a customs post on a main route, which explains a chief tax collector living there.

decisions.choice: was passing through: the action under way when the next event happens
decisions.reason: The imperfect tense shows Jesus in the middle of crossing the town. He meant to go on, which makes his stopping at Zacchaeus' house in 19:5 the more striking.

decisions.choice: Jesus
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name Jesus at the start of a new section.

records.heading: Zacchaeus climbs a tree

records.source: καὶ ἰδοὺ ἀνὴρ ὀνόματι καλούμενος Ζακχαῖος, καὶ αὐτὸς ἦν ἀρχιτελώνης καὶ αὐτὸς πλούσιος·
records.gloss: And look, a man by name being called Zacchaeus, and he was a chief tax collector and he [was] rich;
pieces: A man named Zacchaeus lived there. He was a chief tax collector, and he was rich.

L.2: And look, [there was] a man called by the name Zacchaeus; and he was a chief tax collector, and he [was] rich.

R.2: A man named Zacchaeus lived there. He was the head of the tax collectors in that area, and he was very rich.

decisions.choice: chief tax collector: a man in charge of collecting tolls and taxes in a district, with other collectors working under him
alternatives: a high official of the Roman government
decisions.reason: The word is found nowhere else in Greek writing before Luke, and is built from "chief" and "tax collector". Collectors bid for the right to gather the tolls of an area and kept what they took above the agreed sum (3:12-13). A chief collector probably held the contract and had others collect for him, so he grew rich from their work as well as his own. Tax collectors were despised as cheats and as servants of foreign rulers (5:30; 18:10-13).

decisions.choice: rich: Luke sets this rich man beside the rich ruler of 18:18-25
decisions.reason: Jesus has just said that it is hard for the rich to enter the kingdom of God, but that what is impossible for people is possible for God (18:24-27). Zacchaeus is a rich man who is saved (19:9).

decisions.choice: Zacchaeus: a Jewish name
decisions.reason: The name is a Greek form of a Hebrew name meaning "clean" or "innocent" (Ezra 2:9 has a family of that name). He is a Jew, a son of Abraham (19:9), working in a trade his people despised.

decisions.choice: look (L); not rendered as a separate word, or "now" (B, R)
decisions.reason: Luke uses this word to draw attention to what follows. "Behold" is old-fashioned; Literal says "look", and Balanced and Readable carry the force in the flow of the sentence, as in Matthew 1:20.

decisions.choice: lived there
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say where the man was, as "look" points to someone the reader meets in Jericho.

decisions.choice: the head of the tax collectors in that area
decisions.reason: Readable explains the title (m1).

records.source: καὶ ἐζήτει ἰδεῖν τὸν Ἰησοῦν τίς ἐστιν, καὶ οὐκ ἠδύνατο ἀπὸ τοῦ ὄχλου ὅτι τῇ ἡλικίᾳ μικρὸς ἦν.
records.gloss: and he was seeking to see the Jesus who he is, and not he was able because of the crowd, because in the stature small he was.
pieces: He was trying to see who Jesus was, but he could not see over the crowd, because he was a short man.

L.3: And he was trying to see who Jesus was, and he was not able to because of the crowd, for he was small in stature.

R.3: He wanted to see what Jesus was like. But there were too many people, and Zacchaeus was too short to see over them.

decisions.choice: small in stature: short
decisions.reason: The noun can mean age or height. Here, where he cannot see over a crowd and climbs a tree, it means height.

decisions.choice: he was small: Zacchaeus, not Jesus
decisions.reason: Grammatically "he" could refer to either man. But the one who runs ahead and climbs a tree to see is Zacchaeus, so he is the short one.

decisions.choice: trying to see who Jesus was: wanting to see this man for himself
decisions.reason: The verb "seek" is used again in 19:10, where the Son of Man comes to seek the lost. Zacchaeus is looking for Jesus, but Jesus is the one who finds him.

decisions.choice: too short to see over them; Zacchaeus
decisions.reason: Readable makes plain how his height stopped him seeing and names the short man (m2).

records.source: καὶ προδραμὼν εἰς τὸ ἔμπροσθεν ἀνέβη ἐπὶ συκομορέαν ἵνα ἴδῃ αὐτόν, ὅτι ἐκείνης ἤμελλεν διέρχεσθαι.
records.gloss: And having run ahead to the front he went up onto a sycamore-fig tree in order that he might see him, because that [way] he was about to pass through.
pieces: So he ran on ahead and climbed a sycamore-fig tree to see {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, since Jesus was going to come along that road.

L.4: And running ahead to the front, he climbed up into a sycamore-fig tree so that he might see {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, because {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was about to pass through that [way].

R.4: So he ran on ahead of the crowd and climbed up into a fig tree to see Jesus. Jesus was going to pass that way.

decisions.choice: sycamore-fig: a kind of fig tree with a short trunk and wide, low branches
alternatives: the sycamore or plane tree of northern countries
decisions.reason: This tree grew in the warm lowlands such as the Jordan valley (1 Kings 10:27; Amos 7:14). Its short trunk and spreading low branches made it easy to climb. It is not the tree called sycamore in Europe or North America.

decisions.choice: running ahead: a rich man setting aside his dignity
decisions.reason: Grown men of standing did not run in public or climb trees. Zacchaeus does both to see Jesus.

decisions.choice: that way: along that road
decisions.reason: The word is a pronoun meaning "that one", with "way" or "road" understood.

decisions.choice: Jesus
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name Jesus so that the reader can tell the two men apart.

decisions.choice: fig tree
decisions.reason: Readable keeps it simple; the tree was a kind of fig (m1). Literal and Balanced give its full name.

records.source: καὶ ὡς ἦλθεν ἐπὶ τὸν τόπον, ἀναβλέψας ὁ Ἰησοῦς εἶπεν πρὸς αὐτόν· Ζακχαῖε, σπεύσας κατάβηθι, σήμερον γὰρ ἐν τῷ οἴκῳ σου δεῖ με μεῖναι.
records.gloss: And when he came to the place, having looked up the Jesus said to him, Zacchaeus, having hurried come down, today for in the house of you it is necessary [for] me to stay.
pieces: When Jesus reached the spot, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} looked up and said to him, "Zacchaeus, hurry down. Today is the day I have to stay in your home."

L.5: And when {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} came to the place, Jesus looked up and said to him, "Zacchaeus, hurry [and] come down, for today I must stay at your house."

R.5: When Jesus came to that place, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} looked up at Zacchaeus. He said, "Zacchaeus, come down from there, and be quick! Today I need to stay at your house."

decisions.choice: must: it is God's will that Jesus stay there
decisions.reason: Luke uses this word for what God has planned and Jesus must carry out (2:49; 4:43; 9:22; 13:33). Staying with a tax collector is part of the work Jesus was sent to do (19:10).

decisions.choice: today: salvation comes now
alternatives: only the date of the visit
decisions.reason: "Today" comes again in 19:9: today salvation has come to this house. Luke uses the word for the moment God's salvation arrives (2:11; 4:21; 23:43).

decisions.choice: stay at your house: be his guest, sharing food and perhaps lodging
decisions.reason: To stay in someone's house and eat with him was to accept him. Jesus invites himself, and does it publicly.

decisions.choice: the place: the tree where Zacchaeus was
alternatives: a known place in the town
decisions.reason: The place is the spot on the road beside the tree he had climbed (19:4).

decisions.choice: Today is the day I have to stay
alternatives: I must stay at your house today
decisions.reason: The Greek puts "today" first, for emphasis (m2). Balanced keeps the stress at the start.

records.source: καὶ σπεύσας κατέβη, καὶ ὑπεδέξατο αὐτὸν χαίρων.
records.gloss: And having hurried he came down, and he welcomed him rejoicing.
pieces: So he hurried down and gladly welcomed {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

L.6: And hurrying, he came down, and he welcomed {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, rejoicing.

R.6: So Zacchaeus quickly climbed down. He was very happy to welcome Jesus into his home.

decisions.choice: welcomed: received as a guest
decisions.reason: The verb is used of receiving someone into one's home (10:38; Acts 17:7).

decisions.choice: rejoicing: the joy of those who receive salvation
decisions.reason: Luke often tells of joy when God's salvation comes (1:14; 2:10; 15:5-7, 32). Zacchaeus' gladness is the first sign of what 19:9 announces.

decisions.choice: into his home
decisions.reason: Readable says where he welcomed Jesus (m1).

records.source: καὶ ἰδόντες πάντες διεγόγγυζον λέγοντες ὅτι Παρὰ ἁμαρτωλῷ ἀνδρὶ εἰσῆλθεν καταλῦσαι.
records.gloss: And having seen all were grumbling saying that With a sinful man he has gone in to lodge.
pieces: Everyone who saw it began to mutter and complain. "He has gone to be a guest at the house of a sinner!" they said.

L.7: And seeing [it], all were grumbling, saying, "With a sinful man {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has gone in to lodge!"

R.7: Everyone saw this and began to grumble. They said, "He has gone to stay at the home of a man who is a sinner!"

decisions.choice: were grumbling: complaining among themselves
decisions.reason: The same strong form of the verb is used when Pharisees and scribes complain that Jesus welcomes sinners and eats with them (15:2; compare 5:30). Here "all" grumble, not only the leaders.

decisions.choice: a sinful man: a man known for his sin, here because of his trade
alternatives: a man with a hidden sin
decisions.reason: Tax collectors were counted as sinners because they cheated people and worked for foreign rulers (3:12-13; 5:30; 7:34). A guest shared in his host's standing.

decisions.choice: lodge: stay as a guest
decisions.reason: The verb means to break a journey and find lodging (9:12).

decisions.choice: they said, after the quoted words
decisions.reason: Balanced puts the quotation first and gives the speakers after it.

decisions.choice: He has gone ... (no deity_pronoun setting at the start of the quoted sentence)
decisions.reason: The pronoun means Jesus, but it begins a sentence, so it is capitalized either way.

records.source: σταθεὶς δὲ Ζακχαῖος εἶπεν πρὸς τὸν κύριον· Ἰδοὺ τὰ ἡμίσιά μου τῶν ὑπαρχόντων, κύριε, τοῖς πτωχοῖς δίδωμι, καὶ εἴ τινός τι ἐσυκοφάντησα ἀποδίδωμι τετραπλοῦν.
records.gloss: Having stood then Zacchaeus said to the Lord, Look, the halves of me of the possessions, Lord, to the poor I give, and if of anyone anything I extorted I give back fourfold.
pieces: But Zacchaeus stood up and said to the Lord, "Lord, see: half of what I own I am giving to the poor. And if I have taken anything from anyone by cheating, I am paying it back four times over."

L.8: But Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord, "Look, half of my possessions, Lord, I give to the poor; and if I have extorted anything from anyone, I give back four times as much."

R.8: Zacchaeus stood up and said to the Lord Jesus, "Lord, I will give half of everything I own to poor people. And if I have cheated anyone out of anything, I will pay that person back four times as much."

decisions.choice: I give, I give back: a promise Zacchaeus makes now, which takes effect at once
alternatives: a description of what he already does as his habit, defending himself against the grumbling
decisions.reason: The verbs are in the present tense. Some read them as his regular practice: he already gives half and repays any wrong. But Jesus answers that salvation has come today (19:9), and the story is about a sinner changed by meeting Jesus, so the present is best read as a decision he makes on the spot.

decisions.choice: extorted: got money from someone by threats or false charges
alternatives: made a mistake in the accounts
decisions.reason: The verb is the one John the Baptist used when he told soldiers not to extort money (3:14). "If" does not mean he doubts it; it means "whatever I have taken in this way".

decisions.choice: fourfold: the repayment the law required for a stolen sheep
decisions.reason: The law of Moses required a thief who killed or sold a stolen sheep to repay four sheep (Exodus 22:1; 2 Samuel 12:6). For ordinary wrongs, the law asked the full amount plus a fifth (Leviticus 6:5; Numbers 5:7). Zacchaeus takes on the heaviest penalty.

decisions.choice: the Lord; Lord: Jesus
decisions.reason: Luke the narrator calls Jesus "the Lord" (7:13; 10:1; 18:6), and Zacchaeus addresses him with the same word.

decisions.choice: look (L); not rendered as a separate word, or "now" (B, R)
decisions.reason: Luke uses this word to draw attention to what follows. "Behold" is old-fashioned; Literal says "look", and Balanced and Readable carry the force in the flow of the sentence, as in Matthew 1:20.

decisions.choice: the Lord Jesus
decisions.reason: Readable names Jesus, as at 12:42.

decisions.choice: I will give; I will pay
decisions.reason: Readable gives the sense of the present tense as a promise (m1).

records.source: εἶπεν δὲ πρὸς αὐτὸν ὁ Ἰησοῦς ὅτι Σήμερον σωτηρία τῷ οἴκῳ τούτῳ ἐγένετο, καθότι καὶ αὐτὸς υἱὸς Ἀβραάμ ἐστιν·
records.gloss: Said then to him the Jesus that Today salvation to the house this came, because also he a son of Abraham is;
pieces: Jesus said to him, "Today salvation has come to this household. This man too is one of Abraham's sons.

L.9: And Jesus said to him, "Today salvation has come to this house, because he too is a son of Abraham.

R.9: Jesus said to him, "Today God has brought salvation to this house. This man belongs to God's people too. He is a true son of Abraham.

decisions.choice: salvation: rescue by God, here the forgiveness and new life that come with Jesus
decisions.reason: Zechariah praised God for salvation that comes through the forgiveness of sins (1:69, 77), and Simeon saw that salvation in the child Jesus (2:30). Salvation comes to Zacchaeus' house as Jesus enters it.

decisions.choice: this house: Zacchaeus and his household
decisions.reason: "House" often means the people who live in it (10:5; Acts 16:31).

decisions.choice: he too is a son of Abraham: a Jew, an heir of God's promise to Abraham, despite what people say of him
alternatives: he has become a son of Abraham by giving to the poor
decisions.reason: The crowd treat Zacchaeus as an outsider (19:7). Jesus says he belongs to God's people, to whom God promised mercy (1:54-55, 73). Jesus calls a crippled woman a daughter of Abraham in the same way (13:16).

decisions.choice: to him: to Zacchaeus, with the crowd listening
decisions.reason: Jesus speaks to Zacchaeus but of him in the third person ("he too"), so the words are meant for those who grumbled as well.

decisions.choice: God has brought salvation; This man belongs to God's people too
alternatives: salvation has come; he too is a son of Abraham (alone)
decisions.reason: Readable says who brings salvation and what being a son of Abraham means (m3), and keeps the phrase itself.

decisions.choice: the quotation opens here and closes at the end of 19:10
decisions.reason: The next sentence continues Jesus' words.

records.source: ἦλθεν γὰρ ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ζητῆσαι καὶ σῶσαι τὸ ἀπολωλός.
records.gloss: came for the Son of the Man to seek and to save the [thing] having been lost.
pieces: The Son of Man came to look for what was lost and to save it."

L.10: For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost."

R.10: I, the Son of Man, came to look for people who are lost and to save them."

decisions.choice: to seek and to save the lost: as God promised to seek his lost sheep
alternatives: a general saying with no background
decisions.reason: In Ezekiel 34 God condemns Israel's shepherds, who did not seek the lost, and promises to seek the lost himself and bring them back (Ezekiel 34:4, 16). Jesus does what God said he would do. The parables of the lost sheep, coin and son make the same point (15:4-32).

decisions.choice: the Son of Man: Jesus' name for himself, recalling Daniel 7:13-14
decisions.reason: As in 5:24 and 9:22. Here the title is joined to his mission to save.

decisions.choice: the lost: whatever is lost, here people who have strayed from God
decisions.reason: The form is singular and neuter, "that which has been lost", a general way of speaking of all who are lost, as in 15:4-6 and 15:24, 32.

decisions.choice: I, the Son of Man
decisions.reason: Readable makes clear that Jesus is speaking of himself (m2).

decisions.choice: what was lost (B); people who are lost (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the general sense of the neuter word; Readable says it is about people (m3). Literal has the familiar "the lost".

records.source: Ἀκουόντων δὲ αὐτῶν ταῦτα προσθεὶς εἶπεν παραβολὴν διὰ τὸ ἐγγὺς εἶναι Ἰερουσαλὴμ αὐτὸν καὶ δοκεῖν αὐτοὺς ὅτι παραχρῆμα μέλλει ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ ἀναφαίνεσθαι·
records.gloss: Hearing then of them these [things], having added he spoke a parable because of the near being Jerusalem him and the thinking them that immediately is about the kingdom of the God to appear;
pieces: As they listened to this, Jesus went on to tell them a parable. He did this because {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was near Jerusalem, and they supposed that the kingdom of God was about to appear at once.

L.11: While they were listening to these things, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} went on to tell a parable, because {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was near Jerusalem and they thought that the kingdom of God was going to appear immediately.

R.11: The people were listening to all this. Then Jesus told them a story. He told it because {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was getting close to Jerusalem. The people thought that God was going to set up his kingdom right away.

decisions.choice: having added: went on, adding a parable to what he had said
decisions.reason: The verb means to add. Jesus continues speaking to those who heard his words to Zacchaeus.

decisions.choice: the kingdom of God was going to appear immediately: they expected God's rule to be set up in Jerusalem at once
alternatives: they thought the kingdom was already present
decisions.reason: Jesus was going up to Jerusalem, the city of David. Many expected that the Messiah would take power there and drive out Israel's enemies (24:21; Acts 1:6). The parable tells of a king who goes away and comes back only after a long time.

decisions.choice: they: those who heard Jesus at Zacchaeus' house, including the grumblers
decisions.reason: The pronoun looks back to 19:7-10.

decisions.choice: two sentences: the parable, then the reasons
decisions.reason: The Greek gives the two reasons in one long clause. Balanced and Readable say first that he told a parable, then why.

decisions.choice: a story; God was going to set up his kingdom
alternatives: a parable; the kingdom of God was going to appear
decisions.reason: Readable explains what a parable is and what the people expected (m2).

records.heading: Ten servants and ten minas

records.source: εἶπεν οὖν· Ἄνθρωπός τις εὐγενὴς ἐπορεύθη εἰς χώραν μακρὰν λαβεῖν ἑαυτῷ βασιλείαν καὶ ὑποστρέψαι.
records.gloss: He said therefore, A man certain of noble birth went into a country distant to receive for himself a kingdom and to return.
pieces: So {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said, "A man from a noble family traveled to a faraway country to be made king there, and then to come back home.

L.12: So {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said, "A certain man of noble birth went to a distant country to receive a kingdom for himself and to return.

R.12: Jesus said, "There was once a man from an important family. He went on a long journey to a country far away. He went there so that he could be made king, and then come back home.

decisions.choice: went to a distant country to receive a kingdom: as the rulers of Judea went to Rome to be confirmed as kings
alternatives: he went to conquer a kingdom
decisions.reason: Rulers in the land of Israel held power only by the grant of Rome. When Herod the Great died in 4 BC, his son Archelaus went to Rome to ask the emperor to make him king, and a delegation of Jews followed him to argue against him. Jesus' hearers in Jericho, where Archelaus had built a palace, would know the story.

decisions.choice: a man of noble birth: in the story, a figure for Jesus, who goes away and will return as king
alternatives: only a story about a ruler of the day
decisions.reason: The parable answers the people's belief that the kingdom would appear at once (19:11). Like the nobleman, Jesus will go away and return later, and his servants must be faithful until then (12:35-48).

decisions.choice: kingdom: royal rule, the right to reign as king
decisions.reason: The word means kingship more than land. He returns having received it (19:15).

decisions.choice: the quotation opens here and runs on to the end of 19:27
alternatives: a new quotation for each part of the story
decisions.reason: The whole parable is Jesus' speech. What the people in it say is in single quotation marks.

decisions.choice: to be made king there
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what receiving a kingdom means (m3).

records.source: καλέσας δὲ δέκα δούλους ἑαυτοῦ ἔδωκεν αὐτοῖς δέκα μνᾶς καὶ εἶπεν πρὸς αὐτούς· Πραγματεύσασθε ἐν ᾧ ἔρχομαι.
records.gloss: Having called then ten slaves of himself he gave to them ten minas and said to them, Do business while I come.
pieces: Before he left, he called ten of his servants and gave them ten minas, one to each. 'Put this money to work until I come back,' he told them.

L.13: And calling ten of his slaves, he gave them ten minas and said to them, 'Do business until I come.'

R.13: Before he left, he called ten of his servants. He gave each of them one mina. A mina was an amount of money worth about a hundred days' pay. He told them, 'Use this money to do business until I come back.'

decisions.choice: mina: a sum of money equal to a hundred drachmas, about a hundred days' wages
alternatives: a large fortune, like a talent
decisions.reason: A mina was a weight of silver, not a coin. It was worth a hundred drachmas, and a drachma, like a denarius, was a usual day's pay (15:8; 7:41). So each slave received a modest but real sum, about four months' wages. The parable of the talents in Matthew 25:14-30 speaks of far larger amounts.

decisions.choice: slaves: men owned by the nobleman, who managed his affairs
decisions.reason: The word is the usual word for a slave. In large households trusted slaves often ran business for their master (12:42-43).

decisions.choice: ten slaves, ten minas: one mina each
decisions.reason: Each slave receives the same amount, and later each reports on "your mina" (19:16, 18, 20).

decisions.choice: do business while I come: trade with it until I return
decisions.reason: The verb means to trade or do business. The phrase that follows is an idiom for "while I am on my way", that is, until he comes.

decisions.choice: mina (every level)
decisions.reason: The amount is explained once, in Readable at 19:13 and in the meaning decision there. Repeating a modern sum each time the servants speak would make the dialogue hard to follow, so every level keeps the unit's own name. "Pound", the older rendering, now suggests British money.

decisions.choice: one to each (B); He gave each of them one mina (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable state what the story assumes (m3).

decisions.choice: A mina was an amount of money worth about a hundred days' pay
decisions.reason: Readable explains the amount once, in a sentence of its own, because the word mina is used again and again in the story (m1). A setting span here would leave the later uses unexplained.

decisions.choice: servants
decisions.reason: "Servant" in Balanced and Readable, as the style guide has it; the meaning decision (m2) keeps that the person was owned, and Literal keeps "slave".

records.source: οἱ δὲ πολῖται αὐτοῦ ἐμίσουν αὐτόν, καὶ ἀπέστειλαν πρεσβείαν ὀπίσω αὐτοῦ λέγοντες· Οὐ θέλομεν τοῦτον βασιλεῦσαι ἐφ’ ἡμᾶς.
records.gloss: But the citizens of him were hating him, and they sent a delegation after him saying, Not we want this one to reign over us.
pieces: But the people of his country hated him. They sent a delegation after him to say, 'We do not want this man to be our king.'

L.14: But his citizens hated him, and they sent a delegation after him, saying, 'We do not want this man to reign over us.'

R.14: But the people of his own country hated him. So they sent some men after him with this message: 'We do not want this man to be our king!'

decisions.choice: sent a delegation after him: to the ruler who would grant the kingdom, to argue against him
decisions.reason: So the Jews did when Archelaus went to Rome (19:12). The delegation follows him to the distant country.

decisions.choice: his citizens hated him: in the story, those of his own people who refuse Jesus as their king
decisions.reason: They are his own people. In Jerusalem the leaders will reject Jesus (19:39, 47; 20:14), and in 19:27 the king judges those who would not have him reign.

decisions.choice: were hating: their hatred went on
decisions.reason: The imperfect tense describes a settled attitude.

decisions.choice: to be our king
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use a plain phrase for the verb "reign".

records.source: καὶ ἐγένετο ἐν τῷ ἐπανελθεῖν αὐτὸν λαβόντα τὴν βασιλείαν καὶ εἶπεν φωνηθῆναι αὐτῷ τοὺς δούλους τούτους οἷς δεδώκει τὸ ἀργύριον, ἵνα γνοῖ τί διεπραγματεύσαντο.
records.gloss: And it came about in the returning him having received the kingdom, and he said to be called to him the slaves these to whom he had given the money, in order that he might know what they had gained by trading.
pieces: He was made king and came back home. Then he sent for the servants to whom he had given the money, to find out what profit each had made by his trading.

L.15: And it happened, when he returned after receiving the kingdom, that he gave orders for these slaves to whom he had given the money to be called to him, so that he might know what they had gained by trading.

R.15: He was made king anyway, and he came back home. Then he sent for the servants he had given the money to. He wanted to know how much each of them had earned.

decisions.choice: having received the kingdom: in spite of the delegation, he was made king
alternatives: he received it only after his return
decisions.reason: The participle describes what happened before his return: he went to receive kingship and came back with it.

decisions.choice: had gained by trading: what each had earned through business
decisions.reason: The verb is a strengthened form of the verb "do business" in 19:13, with the sense of carrying business through to a result.

decisions.choice: the money: the silver he had given them
decisions.reason: The word means silver, and so money. It refers to the minas.

decisions.choice: anyway
decisions.reason: Readable shows that the delegation of 19:14 did not stop him (m1).

decisions.choice: servants
decisions.reason: "Servant" in Balanced and Readable (style guide); Literal keeps "slave".

records.source: παρεγένετο δὲ ὁ πρῶτος λέγων· Κύριε, ἡ μνᾶ σου δέκα προσηργάσατο μνᾶς.

L.16: And the first came, saying, 'Master, your mina has earned ten more minas.'

R.16: The first servant came and said, 'Master, I used your mina, and it has earned ten more minas!'

decisions.choice: your mina has earned: the slave credits the result to his master's money
alternatives: the slave boasts of his own skill
decisions.reason: He does not say "I have earned" but "your mina has earned". The gift came from the master.

decisions.choice: has earned more: has produced in addition
decisions.reason: The verb means to earn something more. He now has eleven minas: the original and ten more.

decisions.choice: Master
decisions.reason: As in the parables of 12:36-46, the slaves' owner is called master. In the story the word is the title a slave gives the man who owns him; "Lord" would make him sound like God.

decisions.choice: mina (every level)
decisions.reason: The amount is explained once, in Readable at 19:13 and in the meaning decision there. Repeating a modern sum each time the servants speak would make the dialogue hard to follow, so every level keeps the unit's own name. "Pound", the older rendering, now suggests British money.

decisions.choice: I used your mina, and
decisions.reason: Readable says that the servant had put the money to work.

records.source: καὶ εἶπεν αὐτῷ· Εὖγε, ἀγαθὲ δοῦλε, ὅτι ἐν ἐλαχίστῳ πιστὸς ἐγένου, ἴσθι ἐξουσίαν ἔχων ἐπάνω δέκα πόλεων.
records.gloss: And he said to him, Well done, good slave, because in a very little faithful you were, be authority having over ten cities.

R.17: The king said to him, 'You have done well! You are a good servant. You have shown that I can trust you with a small amount of money. So I will put you in charge of ten cities.'

decisions.choice: well done: words of praise
decisions.reason: The word is an exclamation of approval.

decisions.choice: faithful in a very little: trustworthy with small things, and so given great ones
decisions.reason: Jesus has taught that whoever is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much (16:10), and that the faithful slave will be set over all his master's goods (12:44). A mina is small beside the rule of ten cities.

decisions.choice: faithful: trustworthy, reliable
decisions.reason: The adjective describes a slave who can be trusted, as in 12:42.

decisions.choice: Excellent (B); You have done well (R)
decisions.reason: The familiar "Well done" is kept at Literal; Balanced and Readable use other plain words of praise.

decisions.choice: The king
decisions.reason: Readable names the speaker, who is now king (19:15).

decisions.choice: servant
decisions.reason: "Servant" in Balanced and Readable (style guide); Literal keeps "slave".

decisions.choice: has made: has produced
decisions.reason: A plainer verb than in 19:16, with the same meaning: the mina produced five more.

decisions.choice: Master

decisions.choice: mina (every level)

decisions.choice: I used your mina, and; more
alternatives: your mina has made five minas
decisions.reason: As in 19:16.

records.source: εἶπεν δὲ καὶ τούτῳ· Καὶ σὺ ἐπάνω γίνου πέντε πόλεων.
records.gloss: He said then also to this one, And you over be five cities.
pieces: To him too he said, 'You will be over five cities.'

L.19: And he said also to this one, 'And you, be over five cities.'

R.19: The king said to this servant too, 'I will put you in charge of five cities.'

decisions.choice: five cities: a reward in proportion to what he gained
alternatives: a lesser praise of his work
decisions.reason: This slave gains five and is set over five cities; the first gained ten and is set over ten. The master does not call him "good", but he still rewards him.

decisions.choice: The king; I will put you in charge
decisions.reason: Readable names the speaker and puts the command as a promise, as in 19:17.

records.source: καὶ ὁ ἕτερος ἦλθεν λέγων· Κύριε, ἰδοὺ ἡ μνᾶ σου ἣν εἶχον ἀποκειμένην ἐν σουδαρίῳ·

R.20: Then another servant came and said, 'Master, here is your mina. I wrapped it in a cloth and hid it away.

decisions.choice: the other: the next slave, who stands for the rest
decisions.reason: Ten slaves received money, but the story tells of three. The article marks this one as the next to report.

decisions.choice: a cloth: a small cloth such as one used to wipe the face
decisions.reason: The word means a face cloth or handkerchief (John 11:44; 20:7). Wrapping money in a cloth was a careless way to keep it; burying it was thought safer (Matthew 25:18, 25).

decisions.choice: look (L); not rendered as a separate word, or "now" (B, R)
decisions.reason: Luke uses this word to draw attention to what follows. "Behold" is old-fashioned; Literal says "look", and Balanced and Readable carry the force in the flow of the sentence, as in Matthew 1:20.

decisions.choice: Master
decisions.reason: As in 19:16. In the story the word is the title a slave gives the man who owns him; "Lord" would make him sound like God.

decisions.choice: mina (every level)
decisions.reason: The amount is explained once, in Readable at 19:13 and in the meaning decision there. Repeating a modern sum each time the servants speak would make the dialogue hard to follow, so every level keeps the unit's own name. "Pound", the older rendering, now suggests British money.

decisions.choice: the slave's words continue in 19:21; the single quotation mark closes there
decisions.reason: The sentence continues after the raised dot.

records.source: ἐφοβούμην γάρ σε ὅτι ἄνθρωπος αὐστηρὸς εἶ, αἴρεις ὃ οὐκ ἔθηκας καὶ θερίζεις ὃ οὐκ ἔσπειρας.
records.gloss: I was fearing for you, because a man harsh you are, you take up what not you laid down and you reap what not you sowed.
pieces: I was afraid of you, because you are a severe man. You take out what you never put in, and you harvest what you never planted.'

L.21: For I was afraid of you, because you are a harsh man: you take up what you did not lay down, and you reap what you did not sow.'

R.21: I was afraid of you, because you are a hard man. You take money you did not put in, and you gather crops you did not plant.'

decisions.choice: harsh: strict, exacting
decisions.reason: The word describes someone severe and hard to please, who demands what is owed and more.

decisions.choice: you take up what you did not lay down, and reap what you did not sow: you profit from what others have done
decisions.reason: Both sayings sound like proverbs for someone who gets gain without work of his own. The slave uses them to excuse his fear; the king takes up his words in 19:22.

decisions.choice: for: the reason he kept the money hidden
decisions.reason: "For" explains why he put the money away instead of trading with it.

decisions.choice: take out what you never put in (B); take money you did not put in (R)
alternatives: take up what you did not lay down
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use a picture from money, which fits the story; Literal keeps the wording.

records.source: λέγει αὐτῷ· Ἐκ τοῦ στόματός σου κρίνω σε, πονηρὲ δοῦλε· ᾔδεις ὅτι ἐγὼ ἄνθρωπος αὐστηρός εἰμι, αἴρων ὃ οὐκ ἔθηκα καὶ θερίζων ὃ οὐκ ἔσπειρα;
records.gloss: He says to him, Out of the mouth of you I will judge you, wicked slave; you knew that I a man harsh am, taking up what not I laid down and reaping what not I sowed?
pieces: He answered, 'Your own words condemn you, you wicked servant! So you knew that I am a severe man, taking out what I never put in and harvesting what I never planted?

L.22: He says to him, 'Out of your own mouth I will judge you, wicked slave! You knew that I am a harsh man, taking up what I did not lay down and reaping what I did not sow?

R.22: The king answered, 'You are an evil servant! I will judge you by what you have just said. You say you knew that I am a hard man. You knew that I take money I did not put in, and gather crops I did not plant.

decisions.choice: out of your mouth I will judge you: your own words will be the grounds for my judgment
alternatives: I will judge you for speaking
decisions.reason: The mouth stands for what a person says. The slave's own description of the master shows that he should have acted.

decisions.choice: you knew ...? : a question that takes up the slave's words, not an admission
alternatives: a statement: you knew that I am harsh
decisions.reason: The king repeats the slave's claim to show where it leads (19:23), without agreeing that it is true. The sentence can be read as a question or as a statement; the sense is much the same.

decisions.choice: wicked: evil, worthless
decisions.reason: The word is the usual word for evil. His failure to serve shows what he is.

decisions.choice: he says: the present tense brings the scene close
decisions.reason: Luke uses a present tense here for a past event, as storytellers do; the renderings use the past at Balanced and Readable.

decisions.choice: the charge first, then the servant's own words
decisions.reason: Readable breaks the long question into short statements.

decisions.choice: the king's words continue to the end of 19:23
decisions.reason: The single quotation mark closes at the end of 19:23.

decisions.choice: servant
decisions.reason: "Servant" in Balanced and Readable (style guide); Literal keeps "slave".

records.source: καὶ διὰ τί οὐκ ἔδωκάς μου τὸ ἀργύριον ἐπὶ τράπεζαν;
records.gloss: And why not did you give my the money on a table?
pieces: Then why did you not put my money in the bank?

L.23: And why did you not put my money on a [banker's] table?

R.23: Then why did you not at least put my money in the bank?

decisions.choice: a table: the table of a money-changer or banker
decisions.reason: Bankers did business at tables in public places, changing money and taking deposits on which they paid interest (compare 19:45; Matthew 21:12).

decisions.choice: why did you not ...: even the least effort would have done
alternatives: the bank was the best choice
decisions.reason: If he feared his master, the slave could have done the safest and easiest thing. He did nothing at all.

decisions.choice: at least
decisions.reason: Readable brings out that the bank was the smallest thing he could have done (m2).

records.source: κἀγὼ ἐλθὼν σὺν τόκῳ ἂν αὐτὸ ἔπραξα.
records.gloss: And I having come with interest would it have collected.
pieces: Then when I came back, I would have collected it with interest.'

L.23: And I, having come, would have collected it with interest.'

R.23: Then when I came home, I could have collected it with the interest it had earned.'

decisions.choice: interest: payment for the use of deposited money
decisions.reason: The law forbade Israelites to charge interest on loans to a poor fellow Israelite (Exodus 22:25; Deuteronomy 23:19-20), but bankers paid interest on deposits, as the story assumes.

decisions.choice: would have collected: what would have happened if he had banked it
alternatives: what the king will now do
decisions.reason: The particle with the past tense describes what did not happen.

records.source: καὶ τοῖς παρεστῶσιν εἶπεν· Ἄρατε ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ τὴν μνᾶν καὶ δότε τῷ τὰς δέκα μνᾶς ἔχοντι καὶ εἶπαν αὐτῷ· Κύριε, ἔχει δέκα μνᾶς λέγω ὑμῖν ὅτι παντὶ τῷ ἔχοντι δοθήσεται, ἀπὸ δὲ τοῦ μὴ ἔχοντος καὶ ὃ ἔχει ἀρθήσεται.
records.gloss: And to the [ones] standing by he said, Take from him the mina and give [it] to the [one] the ten minas having \v 25 — and they said to him, Lord, he has ten minas — \v 26 I say to you that to everyone having it will be given, but from the [one] not having even what he has will be taken away.
pieces: Then he said to those standing there, 'Take the mina from him and give it to the one who has ten.'
'Master,' they said, 'he has ten minas already!'
'I tell you, everyone who has will be given more. But the one who has nothing will lose even what {{gender:they have|he has}}.

L.24: And he said to those standing by, 'Take the mina from him and give [it] to the one who has the ten minas.'
L.25: And they said to him, 'Master, he has ten minas!'
L.26: 'I tell you that to everyone who has, [more] will be given; but from the one who does not have, even what {{gender:they have|he has}} will be taken away.

R.24: Then the king said to the men standing near him, 'Take the mina away from this servant. Give it to the servant who has ten minas.'
R.25: They said to him, 'But master, he already has ten minas!'
R.26: The king answered, 'I tell you, people who have something will be given more. But people who have nothing will lose even the little they have.

decisions.choice: 19:25, the bystanders' protest: included, the reading of the SBLGNT
alternatives: 19:25 left out, as in a few manuscripts
decisions.reason: Almost all manuscripts have the verse. A few, among them Codex Bezae, leave it out, perhaps because it interrupts the king's words. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: they said ...; I tell you: the bystanders interrupt, and the king answers them
alternatives: 19:26 is Jesus speaking to his hearers, outside the story
decisions.reason: "I tell you" could be Jesus stepping out of the parable, as in 18:8, 14. But 19:27 goes on with the king's words ("these enemies of mine"), so 19:26 is best read as the king's reply to the protest.

decisions.choice: to everyone who has, more will be given: those who use what God gives receive more; those who do not, lose it
decisions.reason: Jesus said the same about hearing his word (8:18). What a person "has" is what he has made good use of. The slave who did nothing loses even the mina.

decisions.choice: those standing by: attendants of the king
decisions.reason: Those standing by are the king's servants at his court, who carry out his orders.

decisions.choice: will be given; will be taken away: by the king, in the story
decisions.reason: The passives describe what the king does; in the lesson, what God does.

decisions.choice: Master
decisions.reason: As in 19:16. In the story the word is the title a slave gives the man who owns him; "Lord" would make him sound like God.

decisions.choice: mina (every level)
decisions.reason: The amount is explained once, in Readable at 19:13 and in the meaning decision there. Repeating a modern sum each time the servants speak would make the dialogue hard to follow, so every level keeps the unit's own name. "Pound", the older rendering, now suggests British money.

decisions.choice: {{gender:they have|he has}} (L, B); the little they have (R)
decisions.reason: The saying is about anyone; Greek speaks of such a person with a masculine form. Readable uses plural words for people, which need no setting.

decisions.choice: The king answered
decisions.reason: Readable names the speaker of 19:26 (m2).

decisions.choice: the king's words in 19:26 open a quotation that continues to the end of 19:27
decisions.reason: 19:27 goes on with what the king says.

records.source: πλὴν τοὺς ἐχθρούς μου τούτους τοὺς μὴ θελήσαντάς με βασιλεῦσαι ἐπ’ αὐτοὺς ἀγάγετε ὧδε καὶ κατασφάξατε αὐτοὺς ἔμπροσθέν μου.
records.gloss: But the enemies of me these, the [ones] not having wanted me to reign over them, bring here and slaughter them before me.
pieces: As for these enemies of mine who did not want me as their king, bring them here and execute them in my presence.'"

L.27: But these enemies of mine, who did not want me to reign over them, bring here and slay them before me.'"

R.27: And bring here those enemies of mine who did not want me to be their king. Kill them right here in front of me!'"

decisions.choice: these enemies: in the story, the citizens who rejected the king; Jesus warns of judgment on those who reject him
decisions.reason: The words belong to the king in the story, and they finish what began in 19:14. Kings of the time often put rebels to death when they took power. Jesus is about to enter Jerusalem, where he will weep over the city's coming judgment (19:41-44).

decisions.choice: slaughter: kill, put to death
decisions.reason: The verb is a strong one, used of slaughtering animals and of killing in battle.

decisions.choice: but: now turning to another matter
decisions.reason: The word marks a change of subject: from the slaves to the enemies.

decisions.choice: the parable ends here, closing the king's words and Jesus' speech
decisions.reason: Jesus' speech began at 19:12.

records.source: Καὶ εἰπὼν ταῦτα ἐπορεύετο ἔμπροσθεν ἀναβαίνων εἰς Ἱεροσόλυμα.

L.28: And having said these things, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} went on ahead, going up to Jerusalem.

R.28: When Jesus had finished telling this story, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} went on ahead of the others on the road up to Jerusalem.

decisions.choice: going up to Jerusalem: climbing from Jericho to the city
decisions.reason: Jerusalem stands in the hills, and the road from Jericho climbs steeply. People spoke of going up to Jerusalem whatever direction they came from (2:42; 18:31).

decisions.choice: went on ahead: leading the way to the city where he would suffer

decisions.choice: of them (B); of the others (R)

records.heading: The king comes riding on a colt

records.source: Καὶ ἐγένετο ὡς ἤγγισεν εἰς Βηθφαγὴ καὶ Βηθανίαν πρὸς τὸ ὄρος τὸ καλούμενον Ἐλαιῶν, ἀπέστειλεν δύο τῶν μαθητῶν λέγων· Ὑπάγετε εἰς τὴν κατέναντι κώμην, ἐν ᾗ εἰσπορευόμενοι εὑρήσετε πῶλον δεδεμένον, ἐφ’ ὃν οὐδεὶς πώποτε ἀνθρώπων ἐκάθισεν, καὶ λύσαντες αὐτὸν ἀγάγετε.
records.gloss: And it came about as he drew near to Bethphage and Bethany toward the mount the [one] being called of Olives, he sent two of the disciples \v 30 saying, Go into the opposite village, in which entering you will find a colt having been tied, on which no one ever of men has sat, and having untied it bring [it].
pieces: As {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} came near Bethphage and Bethany, by the hill called the Mount of Olives, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} sent off two of the disciples.
"Go to the village ahead of you," {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} told them. "As you go into it, you will find a young donkey tied there, one that nobody has ever ridden. Untie it and bring it here.

L.29: And it happened, as {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} drew near to Bethphage and Bethany, at the mount that is called [the Mount] of Olives, [that] {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} sent two of the disciples,
L.30: saying, "Go into the village opposite, where on entering you will find a colt tied, on which no one has ever yet sat. Untie it and bring [it].

R.29: Jesus came near the villages of Bethphage and Bethany, at the hill called the Mount of Olives. There {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} sent two of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} followers ahead.
R.30: He said to them, "Go into the village in front of you. As soon as you go in, you will find a young donkey tied up. No one has ever ridden it. Untie it and bring it to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}.

decisions.choice: Bethphage and Bethany, the Mount of Olives: villages on the hill east of Jerusalem, on the road from Jericho
decisions.reason: The Mount of Olives faces Jerusalem across the Kidron valley. Bethany lay about two miles from the city (John 11:18), and Bethphage was nearer. Zechariah 14:4 speaks of the LORD standing on the Mount of Olives on the day he comes.

decisions.choice: colt: a young animal, here a young donkey
decisions.reason: The word means the young of an animal. Mark 11:2 and John 12:14-15 show it was a donkey, as in Zechariah 9:9, where Zion's king comes humble and riding on a donkey, on a colt.

decisions.choice: on which no one has ever sat: an animal not yet used, fit for a sacred purpose
decisions.reason: Animals set apart for God were ones that had never been put to work (Numbers 19:2; Deuteronomy 21:3; 1 Samuel 6:7).

decisions.choice: the colt: Jesus comes as the king of Zechariah 9:9
decisions.reason: Jesus had walked all the way from Galilee. Riding into the city on a colt acts out the prophecy of the humble king (Zechariah 9:9), which Matthew 21:5 and John 12:15 quote.

decisions.choice: young donkey
decisions.reason: Today a colt is usually a young horse. Balanced and Readable say what animal it was (m2); Literal keeps "colt".

decisions.choice: Jesus' words open here and continue to the end of 19:31
decisions.reason: His instructions go on in 19:31.

decisions.choice: to me
decisions.reason: Readable says where to bring it.

decisions.choice: if anyone asks: the first half of one instruction, finished in the next sentence
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT ends the sentence at the question mark of the quoted question; the answer follows in the next sentence.

decisions.choice: no closing double quotation mark; Jesus' words continue
decisions.reason: The instruction is finished in 19:31b.

records.source: οὕτως ἐρεῖτε ὅτι Ὁ κύριος αὐτοῦ χρείαν ἔχει.

L.31: you shall say this: 'The Lord has need of it.'"

decisions.choice: the Lord: Jesus
decisions.reason: The disciples speak of Jesus by the title Luke uses of him (19:8). Some take it to mean God, or the colt's owner if he was with Jesus, but the owners are in the village (19:33). The words are spoken with authority, as the king claims what he needs.

decisions.choice: of it: the Lord needs the colt
alternatives: the Lord of it, its owner
decisions.reason: The pronoun goes with "need", not with "Lord".

records.source: ἀπελθόντες δὲ οἱ ἀπεσταλμένοι εὗρον καθὼς εἶπεν αὐτοῖς.

decisions.choice: the two disciples
decisions.reason: Readable says who they were (19:29).

decisions.choice: young donkey; donkey
decisions.reason: As in 19:30.

pieces: They answered, "The Lord needs it."

L.34: And they said, "The Lord has need of it."

decisions.choice: the Lord: Jesus, as in 19:31
decisions.reason: The disciples give the answer Jesus told them to give, and the owners let them go. Luke contrasts the owners with the Lord who has a greater claim.

records.source: καὶ ἤγαγον αὐτὸν πρὸς τὸν Ἰησοῦν, καὶ ἐπιρίψαντες αὐτῶν τὰ ἱμάτια ἐπὶ τὸν πῶλον ἐπεβίβασαν τὸν Ἰησοῦν·
records.gloss: And they brought it to the Jesus, and having thrown of them the cloaks on the colt they set on [it] the Jesus;
pieces: They brought the donkey to Jesus, threw their cloaks over it, and helped Jesus get on.

L.35: And they brought it to Jesus, and throwing their cloaks on the colt, they set Jesus on [it].

R.35: They brought the young donkey to Jesus. They put their coats on the donkey's back, and they helped Jesus get up on it.

decisions.choice: cloaks: outer garments, used here as a saddle
decisions.reason: The cloak was the outer robe, worn over the tunic and used as a blanket at night (6:29). The disciples use theirs to make a seat for Jesus.

decisions.choice: they set Jesus on it: as Solomon was set on David's mule to be made king
decisions.reason: When Solomon was to be made king, David had him ride on the king's own mule into the city (1 Kings 1:33-40). Jesus is honored as a king by his followers.

decisions.choice: helped Jesus get on
decisions.reason: The verb means to put someone on a mount. Balanced and Readable say it in plain words.

decisions.choice: coats
decisions.reason: Readable uses a common word for the outer garment.

records.source: πορευομένου δὲ αὐτοῦ ὑπεστρώννυον τὰ ἱμάτια ἑαυτῶν ἐν τῇ ὁδῷ.
records.gloss: Going then of him they were spreading the cloaks of themselves on the road.
pieces: As {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} rode along, people spread their cloaks on the road.

L.36: And as {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} went along, they were spreading their cloaks on the road.

R.36: As Jesus rode along, people spread their coats on the road in front of {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

decisions.choice: spreading their cloaks on the road: honoring a new king
decisions.reason: When Jehu was anointed king, the commanders spread their cloaks under him and proclaimed him king (2 Kings 9:13). The people greet Jesus as king.

decisions.choice: they were spreading: people kept spreading them as he went
decisions.reason: The imperfect describes something done again and again along the way. Luke does not mention branches, as Matthew 21:8 and Mark 11:8 do.

decisions.choice: in front of him
decisions.reason: Readable says where they spread them.

records.source: ἐγγίζοντος δὲ αὐτοῦ ἤδη πρὸς τῇ καταβάσει τοῦ Ὄρους τῶν Ἐλαιῶν ἤρξαντο ἅπαν τὸ πλῆθος τῶν μαθητῶν χαίροντες αἰνεῖν τὸν θεὸν φωνῇ μεγάλῃ περὶ πασῶν ὧν εἶδον δυνάμεων, λέγοντες· Εὐλογημένος ὁ ἐρχόμενος βασιλεὺς ἐν ὀνόματι κυρίου· ἐν οὐρανῷ εἰρήνη καὶ δόξα ἐν ὑψίστοις.
records.gloss: Drawing near then of him already at the descent of the Mount of the Olives they began all the multitude of the disciples rejoicing to praise the God with a voice loud for all which they had seen mighty works, \v 38 saying, Blessed the coming king in [the] name of [the] Lord; in heaven peace and glory in highest [places].
pieces: As {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} came close to the city, where the road goes down the Mount of Olives, the whole crowd of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} disciples began to praise God joyfully and loudly for all the mighty deeds they had seen.
They shouted, "Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord! Peace in heaven, and glory in the highest!"

L.37: And as {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was now drawing near, at the descent of the Mount of Olives, the whole multitude of the disciples began, rejoicing, to praise God with a loud voice for all the works of power that they had seen,
L.38: saying, "Blessed [is] the King who comes in [the] name of [the] Lord! In heaven peace, and glory in [the] highest!"

R.37: Jesus came near the place where the road goes down from the Mount of Olives to Jerusalem. There the whole crowd of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} followers began to praise God. They were full of joy, and they shouted loudly to thank God for all the miracles they had seen.
R.38: They said, "Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord! There is peace in heaven, and glory to God in the highest heaven!"

decisions.choice: Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord: Psalm 118:26, with "the King" added; in the Hebrew, "Lord" is the divine name
decisions.reason: Psalm 118 was sung by pilgrims at the great festivals. Its verse 26 blesses the one who comes in the name of the LORD; the disciples add "the King". Jesus himself quoted the verse in 13:35. To come in the Lord's name is to come sent by God and with his authority.

decisions.choice: blessed: praised, spoken well of before God
decisions.reason: This is not the word of the beatitudes (6:20-22), which says someone is fortunate, but the word used for praising God (1:68) and for those on whom God's blessing rests (1:42).

decisions.choice: peace in heaven, and glory in the highest: peace with God is settled in heaven, and God is praised there
alternatives: a wish: let there be peace in heaven
decisions.reason: The words echo the angels' song at Jesus' birth: glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace (2:14). Here the disciples speak of peace in heaven. God has made peace through the king who comes, and heaven gives him the glory. Luke does not have the cry "Hosanna" found in the other Gospels.

decisions.choice: works of power: miracles
decisions.reason: As in 10:13, the word means acts that show power.

decisions.choice: the descent of the Mount of Olives: where the road from Bethany crests the hill and Jerusalem comes into view
decisions.reason: From the top of the Mount of Olives the road goes down toward the city, which lies across the valley in full view (19:41).

decisions.choice: the whole multitude of the disciples: the large company of his followers, not only the twelve
decisions.reason: Luke speaks of a great company of disciples (6:17). These, not the city crowd, praise him; the Pharisees ask him to silence his disciples (19:39).

decisions.choice: peace; glory (every level)
decisions.reason: Key terms keep the same words at every level.

decisions.choice: There is peace in heaven; glory to God in the highest heaven
alternatives: Peace in heaven, and glory in the highest
decisions.reason: Readable makes a sentence of the first cry and names God as the one given glory, as in 2:14 (m3).

decisions.choice: the Lord
decisions.reason: As at John 1:23: in the New Testament the Greek word "Lord" is rendered "Lord"; meaning decision m1 notes that the Hebrew of Psalm 118 has the divine name.

decisions.choice: mighty deeds (B); miracles (R)
decisions.reason: As in 10:13.

records.source: καί τινες τῶν Φαρισαίων ἀπὸ τοῦ ὄχλου εἶπαν πρὸς αὐτόν· Διδάσκαλε, ἐπιτίμησον τοῖς μαθηταῖς σου.
records.gloss: And some of the Pharisees from the crowd said to him, Teacher, rebuke the disciples of you.
pieces: Some Pharisees in the crowd said to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Teacher, tell {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} disciples to stop!"

L.39: And some of the Pharisees from the crowd said to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Teacher, rebuke {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} disciples!"

R.39: Some of the Pharisees in the crowd said to Jesus, "Teacher, make {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} followers be quiet!"

decisions.choice: Pharisees: a Jewish movement devoted to keeping God's law in every part of life
decisions.reason: As explained at 5:17. This is the last time Luke's Gospel mentions them. They object to the disciples hailing Jesus as king, perhaps fearing the Roman governor's response, or because they reject the claim.

decisions.choice: rebuke: order to stop, correct sternly
decisions.reason: The word is used for a sharp command to stop (9:21, 42; 18:15, 39).

decisions.choice: Teacher: a respectful title, but no more
decisions.reason: The Pharisees call him teacher while the disciples call him king (7:40).

decisions.choice: tell your disciples to stop (B); make your followers be quiet (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what the rebuke would do (m2).

records.source: καὶ ἀποκριθεὶς εἶπεν· Λέγω ὑμῖν, ὅτι ἐὰν οὗτοι σιωπήσουσιν, οἱ λίθοι κράξουσιν.
records.gloss: And answering he said, I say to you, that if these will be silent, the stones will cry out.
pieces: He answered, "I tell you, if these people were silent, the very stones would shout."

L.40: And answering, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said, "I tell you that if these keep silent, the stones will cry out."

R.40: Jesus answered, "I tell you, if my followers stopped praising, the stones themselves would start shouting!"

decisions.choice: the stones will cry out: the praise cannot be stopped; creation itself would give it
alternatives: the stones will cry out against Jerusalem in judgment
decisions.reason: The saying is a vivid way of saying that this moment must be greeted with praise. Habakkuk 2:11 speaks of a stone crying out from the wall against wrongdoing, which some hear here as a hint of judgment, and stones appear again in 19:44.

decisions.choice: if these will be silent: the future tense after "if" pictures a real possibility
alternatives: if these were to be silent
decisions.reason: The construction is unusual. The sense is the same: should the disciples be silent.

decisions.choice: that: introduces what Jesus says
decisions.reason: The word marks the start of the statement after "I tell you".

decisions.choice: would shout (B); would start shouting (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable state the case as a supposition, which fits the sense (m2).

decisions.choice: my followers stopped praising
decisions.reason: Readable says who "these" are and what they would stop doing.

records.source: Καὶ ὡς ἤγγισεν, ἰδὼν τὴν πόλιν ἔκλαυσεν ἐπ’ αὐτήν, λέγων ὅτι Εἰ ἔγνως ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ταύτῃ καὶ σὺ τὰ πρὸς εἰρήνην νῦν δὲ ἐκρύβη ἀπὸ ὀφθαλμῶν σου.
records.gloss: And as he drew near, having seen the city he wept over it, \v 42 saying that If you had known in the day this even you the [things] for peace; but now it was hidden from eyes of you.
pieces: When {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} came nearer and saw the city, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} wept over it.
"If only you too had known on this day the things that lead to peace!" {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said. "But now they are hidden from your sight.

L.41: And as {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} drew near, seeing the city, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} wept over it,
L.42: saying, "If you, even you, had known on this day the things that make for peace! But now they have been hidden from your eyes.

R.41: As Jesus came closer to Jerusalem, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} saw the city, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} cried over it.
R.42: He said, "Jerusalem, I wish that today you had understood what would bring you peace! But now it is hidden from you, and you cannot see it.

decisions.choice: if you had known ...: a wish left unfinished, an expression of grief
alternatives: a condition with its result left out, "it would have saved you"
decisions.reason: The sentence begins as a condition and breaks off. It works as a cry of sorrow: if only you had known.

decisions.choice: the things for peace: what would bring peace with God and safety
alternatives: only a peace treaty with Rome
decisions.reason: The disciples have just sung of peace in heaven (19:38). Jerusalem's name was linked with peace (Hebrews 7:2; Psalm 122:6-8), but the city does not recognize the one who brings it. The war of 19:43-44 shows what follows.

decisions.choice: it was hidden: the way to peace is now hidden from the city
decisions.reason: The passive does not say who hid it. In Scripture God sometimes hides what people refuse to see (Isaiah 6:9-10; Luke 8:10; 18:34).

decisions.choice: wept: cried aloud
decisions.reason: The verb is used of loud weeping (6:21; 7:13; 8:52). Jesus grieves over the city that will reject him.

decisions.choice: on this day: the day the king comes to the city
decisions.reason: "This day" is the day of Jesus' coming; 19:44 calls it the time of the city's visitation.

decisions.choice: peace (every level)
decisions.reason: A key term (m2).

decisions.choice: Jerusalem
decisions.reason: Readable names the city Jesus speaks to.

decisions.choice: Jesus' words open here and close at the end of 19:44
decisions.reason: The next sentence continues his words.

records.heading: Jesus weeps over Jerusalem

records.source: ὅτι ἥξουσιν ἡμέραι ἐπὶ σὲ καὶ παρεμβαλοῦσιν οἱ ἐχθροί σου χάρακά σοι καὶ περικυκλώσουσίν σε καὶ συνέξουσίν σε πάντοθεν, καὶ ἐδαφιοῦσίν σε καὶ τὰ τέκνα σου ἐν σοί, καὶ οὐκ ἀφήσουσιν λίθον ἐπὶ λίθον ἐν σοί, ἀνθ’ ὧν οὐκ ἔγνως τὸν καιρὸν τῆς ἐπισκοπῆς σου.
records.gloss: because will come days upon you and will throw up the enemies of you a palisade against you and will surround you and will hem in you from every side, \v 44 and will dash to the ground you and the children of you in you, and not will they leave stone upon stone in you, because not you knew the time of the visitation of you.
pieces: For a time is coming for you when your enemies will build a siege wall against you. They will encircle you and press in on you from all sides.
They will level you to the ground, you and your children inside you. They will leave no stone on top of another within you, because you did not recognize the time when God came to visit you."

L.43: For days will come upon you when your enemies will set up a palisade against you and surround you and hem you in on every side,
L.44: and they will dash you to the ground, and your children within you, and they will not leave stone upon stone in you, because you did not know the time of your visitation."

R.43: The time is coming when your enemies will build a wall around you. They will surround you and close in on you from every side.
R.44: They will destroy you completely, and they will kill the people who live inside your walls. They will not leave even one stone on top of another. This will happen because you did not understand that God had come to save you."

decisions.choice: palisade: a siege wall of stakes and earth built around a city
decisions.reason: Besiegers built such walls to cut a city off. In AD 70 the Roman army under Titus surrounded Jerusalem with a siege wall, took the city and destroyed the temple.

decisions.choice: dash you to the ground, and your children: the language of the prophets for a city's fall
decisions.reason: The words recall Isaiah 29:3 (the LORD will besiege Jerusalem with siegeworks), Psalm 137:9 and Hosea 10:14 (children dashed down). "Your children" means the city's people.

decisions.choice: the time of your visitation: the time when God came to you
decisions.reason: In the Old Testament God "visits" his people to help or to judge them. Zechariah praised God for visiting his people to redeem them (1:68, 78), and the crowd at Nain said God had visited his people (7:16). Jerusalem did not see that God had come to it in Jesus.

decisions.choice: not leave stone upon stone: destroy completely
alternatives: only the temple will be destroyed
decisions.reason: The city will be so ruined that its buildings fall stone from stone. Jesus says the same of the temple in 21:6.

decisions.choice: the time when God came to visit you (B); that God had come to save you (R)
decisions.reason: "Visitation" is no longer used in this sense. Balanced says who came; Readable says why he came, as in 1:68 and 7:16 (m3). Literal keeps "visitation".

decisions.choice: destroy you completely; kill the people who live inside your walls
alternatives: dash to the ground you and your children
decisions.reason: Readable explains the picture (m2).

records.source: Καὶ εἰσελθὼν εἰς τὸ ἱερὸν ἤρξατο ἐκβάλλειν τοὺς πωλοῦντας, λέγων αὐτοῖς· Γέγραπται· Καὶ ἔσται ὁ οἶκός μου οἶκος προσευχῆς, ὑμεῖς δὲ αὐτὸν ἐποιήσατε σπήλαιον λῃστῶν.
records.gloss: And having entered into the temple he began to drive out the [ones] selling, \v 46 saying to them, It has been written, And will be the house of me a house of prayer, but you it made a cave of robbers.
pieces: Then Jesus went into the temple and began to throw out the people who were selling there.
He said to them, "Scripture says, 'My house will be a house of prayer.' But you have turned it into a hideout for robbers."

L.45: And entering the temple, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} began to drive out those who were selling,
L.46: saying to them, "It is written, 'And {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} house shall be a house of prayer,' but you have made it a cave of robbers."

R.45: Jesus went into the temple courts and began to force out the people who were selling things there.
R.46: He said to them, "The Scriptures say, 'My house will be a place where people pray.' But you have made it a hiding place for robbers!"

decisions.choice: the temple: the whole temple area with its outer courts, where animals for sacrifice were sold
decisions.reason: The word means the temple with its courts. Traders sold animals and birds for the sacrifices and changed money for the temple tax in the outer court.

decisions.choice: my house shall be a house of prayer: Isaiah 56:7
decisions.reason: In Isaiah 56:7 God promises that foreigners who hold fast to his covenant will be brought to his holy mountain, for his house will be called a house of prayer for all peoples. "My" is God speaking. Luke quotes the first part only.

decisions.choice: a cave of robbers: Jeremiah 7:11
decisions.reason: Jeremiah stood at the temple gate and asked whether the house called by God's name had become a robbers' cave in the people's eyes, because they sinned and then came to the temple as if it made them safe (Jeremiah 7:1-15). Robbers hide in caves between their raids. Jeremiah went on to warn that the temple would be destroyed.

decisions.choice: those who were selling: the reading of the SBLGNT
alternatives: those who were selling in it and those who were buying, as in many later manuscripts
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts add "in it, and those who were buying", which matches Mark 11:15. The shorter text has early support. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: robbers: bandits who take by force
decisions.reason: The word means a bandit or armed robber, as in 10:30.

decisions.choice: a cave of robbers (L); a hideout for robbers (B); a hiding place for robbers (R)
decisions.reason: "Den" is now used mostly of an animal's lair, and "thieves" is weaker than the word. The renderings say what a robbers' cave was for (m3).

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} (L); My, capitalized either way at the start of the quotation (B, R)
decisions.reason: God is the speaker in Isaiah 56:7.

decisions.choice: a place where people pray
decisions.reason: Readable says what the phrase means.

decisions.choice: temple courts
decisions.reason: Readable makes clear that the selling was in the courts (m1).

records.heading: A house of prayer

records.source: Καὶ ἦν διδάσκων τὸ καθ’ ἡμέραν ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ· οἱ δὲ ἀρχιερεῖς καὶ οἱ γραμματεῖς ἐζήτουν αὐτὸν ἀπολέσαι καὶ οἱ πρῶτοι τοῦ λαοῦ, καὶ οὐχ εὕρισκον τὸ τί ποιήσωσιν, ὁ λαὸς γὰρ ἅπας ἐξεκρέματο αὐτοῦ ἀκούων.
records.gloss: And he was teaching day by day in the temple; but the chief priests and the scribes were seeking him to destroy and the leading [men] of the people, \v 48 and not they were finding what they might do, the people for all were hanging on him listening.
pieces: Every day {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} taught in the temple. The chief priests and the scribes wanted to kill {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, and so did the leaders of the people.
But they could find no way to do it, because all the people clung to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, listening to every word.

L.47: And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was teaching daily in the temple. But the chief priests and the scribes were seeking to destroy {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, and [so were] the leading men of the people,
L.48: and they did not find what they might do, for all the people were hanging on {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, listening.

R.47: Every day Jesus taught in the temple courts. The chief priests and the teachers of the law wanted to kill {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}. The other leaders of the people wanted this too.
R.48: But they could not find a way to do it, because all the people were listening closely to everything {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said.

decisions.choice: the chief priests, the scribes, the leading men of the people: the groups that made up the ruling council
decisions.reason: The senior priests, the experts in the law and the leading laymen of Jerusalem formed the council that would hand Jesus over (9:22; 22:66). Jesus had foretold that these men would reject him.

decisions.choice: were hanging on him, listening: listened eagerly, holding on to every word
decisions.reason: The verb pictures someone hanging from a support. The people held on to Jesus' words, and their support kept the leaders from acting openly.

decisions.choice: destroy: put to death
decisions.reason: The verb is used for killing (6:9; 17:27).

decisions.choice: was teaching day by day: his regular practice during these days
decisions.reason: Luke describes Jesus' daily teaching in the temple (21:37-38; 22:53).

decisions.choice: the chief priests and the teachers of the law (R); the chief priests and the scribes (L, B)
decisions.reason: As in 9:22: "scribes" today suggests people who copy documents, so Readable says what these men did.

decisions.choice: clung to him, listening to every word
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the picture of holding on (m2) in plainer words.
